en: If we leave this one unwatched,
He seems the kind who will slaughter us!
Zhöözheldet spoke these words,
Saying that the son of Manas had come.
Dwelling himself in Kyzyl-Kyya,
Muradyl, the son of Kyrym,
Was called a hero greater than the Chinese.
His wrestling strength was beyond measure,
His valor was of another order.
He was a lord, he was a khan,
And such a calamitous man.
When he heard this news,
He drew himself up like a blue tiger,
And those who saw him despaired of life.
Wrapping himself in his blue-gray coat,
If you had seen Muradyl,
He raged like a blue lion;
At the word “enemy” he made ready,
Settled into his wrath,
And fastened on all his weapons.
He tensed himself and thundered,
Roaring in true fury.
At the sight, one’s senses scattered;
Blue flame poured from his mouth.
His anger rose and his soul burned,
And his rage grew fierce.
The Manchu standing beside him—
The valiant Muradyl
Struck him down and killed him.
Do not ask what Muradyl was like:
He was a mighty weather-making slave.
He saddled his own Ker Küröng
And had studied the wondrous arts.
His courage was rare, his venom strong;
He was khan of the Soloon people.
Abandon all hope before this infidel!
He was a formidable hero,
One who stood barring the enemy’s advance.
He wore his sword fitted close,
And occupied the borders of the land.
On the slopes of Kyzyl-Kyya,
At the edge of a perilous enemy land,
He oppressed travelers
And abused every merchant he saw;
By the roadside he continually
Dealt out humiliation.
Every person within his reach
He abused and crushed,
Taking whatever they possessed.
He had a grievance to speak of,
And vengeance for his father,
Who had been killed in the Great Campaign.
When he heard this news,
Distress fell upon him and he started in alarm;
He saddled Ker Küröng
And turned all his thoughts to battle.
Beneath him was Ker Küröng—
That surpassing thoroughbred beast,
The offspring of a bay stallion.
Zhöözheldet then spoke a word,
And into the heart of hero Muradyl
He planted a foul word.
Muradyl assembled his wrestlers,
Ordered his warriors to prepare,
And, parting from the Soloons,
His bulk appearing like a mountain,
Climbed the dark-necked ridge,
Up onto its looming spur.
There Muradyl took his place.
When he went out to keep watch,
Hoping his people remained safe,
The tent showed pale in the distance.
When he saw that tent,
Muradyl stood astonished,
And his mind was sorely troubled.
In shape and splendor,
The figure within the tent
Appeared to be the bloodthirsty one’s son!
Muradyl pondered his course.
Against a bloodthirsty man like his father,
Against a trickster like his father,
He could not prevail in combat,
Nor would his strength suffice in wrestling.
If he matched himself against that killer,
He thought it would carry him to his very end;
If the blood-drinker’s descendant
Should chance to capture him,
He would bind him and take him to the Buruts.
Muradyl thought through all of this;
He did not leave any of it unconsidered.
Standing there, Muradyl resolved
To unleash an upheaval:
He would make snow fall
And raid away their horses.
What did hero Muradyl do?
He began to enchant the weather.
Taking the weather-stone he had chosen,
He recited its true spell many times
On the heights of Kyzyl-Kyya;
At Lake Turuna,
He struck the weather-stone into the lake
And began enchanting the weather.
The cloud’s name was Buurakan—
He called it by its name;
The wind’s name was Zhelshamal—
He called it by its name.
A cloud that traveled in winter
He seized in the middle of summer.
The great Chinese warrior Muradyl
Worked measureless weather magic.
Mist formed in the ravines;
Above the mountain peaks,
Black clouds gathered in fury,
Shrieking along the lower slopes,
And black rain closed in.
Above Orgochor,
A towering cloud appeared;
It swept howling over the foothills,
Pouring down blue-blazed hail.
The earth rumbled and shuddered;
From the sky the blue-blazed hail
Came whispering down.
The sullen cloud split apart,
And hailstones as large as bowls poured from the sky.
Nothing could be discerned by sight;
A dark ground fog moved about,
And the face of the earth disappeared.
The ground broke apart with a roar;
Through ravines and hollows,
A flood surged, thundering.
Black cliffs collapsed and crags flowed;
The torrent covered all, and the mountains flowed,
Choking every hollow
And breaking down the riverbanks in heaps.
He turned the summer day to winter;
Before your lord,
Ice stood four fingers thick.
All fourteen horses
Bucked and screamed like foals;
Every one of their halters
Snapped apart,
Bursting wholly into pieces.
The wide world became narrow,
And then the face of the earth
Lay under snow up to the saddlecloths.
(The gray wolves longed
For a single glimpse of the earth’s face.)
Crusted snowdrifts gathered in the hollows;
Living creatures and beasts
Were struck by hail and killed.
Semetey’s Narbuurul
And Khan Bakai’s Kökcholok—
Those two alone remained tethered.
As for the other horses,
Kulchoro and Kanchoro
Turned them loose and drove them on.
The whirlwind of the weather raged fiercely;
Muradyl had brought this calamity.
All fourteen horses together,
Muradyl, the son of Kyrym—
That scoundrel drove them thundering
And raided every one away.
He reached them all together;
Muradyl drove all fourteen horses,
Beating them onward in a single herd,
And raided every one away.
He concealed them at Chaar-Zhon,
Drove them over Üch-Kashka,
And made them cross Sary-Zhaz.
All fourteen horses,
Muradyl raided and took away,
Reaching his home together with them.
The mist scattered from the steppe;
A cold wind blew with a shriek,
And God’s day cleared.
Black steam rose billowing from the earth;
From the wooded hollows,
Larks sang and trilled.
The clouds dispersed one by one,
Breaking apart and going in every direction,
And the world appeared bright again.
Your elder Bakai, that noble lion,
Came out of the tent and looked;
Seeking to know whether the horses were safe,
He saw Kökcholok and Taibuurul—
Those two remained at the tethering place.
They champed upon their bits
And slapped their armfuls of tail
Against their hind legs.
Flattening the right ear,
They flung the crust of the black earth
Up toward the sky.
Two thoroughbreds remained safe;
Apart from them, the fourteen horses
Could nowhere be caught by the eye,
And no one knew where they had gone!
Those fourteen horses were gone;
After the fourteen horses,
The two orphans too were gone!
Then old Bakai
Tore at his beard and flung it aside:
“Alas, if only Manas had not died,
So Bakai need not live to see this shame!
If only God had taken this old man,
And this wretched soul had not lived into old age!
While my mighty Manas was alive,
If only this miserable Bakai had died,
And, never parted from those falcons,
Had looked upon the face of Judgment Day!
If one rode for six months upon the road—
Alas, on such a grievous day,
If only the horse would never tire!
Until he departed for the other world,
If only a hero would never grow old!
Why did I not long ago behold
The narrow road of Judgment Day?”
While my mighty Manas was alive,
Why did I not die then?!
It is the whiteness of my beard:
The children would not heed my words;
It was their time to leave on the journey!
It is the whiteness of my mustache:
When your Bakai was choked with grief,
It was time for him to vanish,
No longer remaining in this world!
While my mighty gray wolf was alive,
Bakai knew the ways of a campaign;
This wretched soul led not merely three boys,
But went at the head of a countless host!
While my lion was alive,
Manas would heed my words;
All the Forty Companions,
Their elders led by Kyrgyl,
When they heard my shout,
Would collapse where they stood!
I was a tulpar traveling the road,
But now I have grown weary.
Parted from my falcon,
No longer counted among the living,
I have grown old!
The city of Kakan-Beijing,
When I held it,
The kalday and jang-jun,
When I beat them down,
While the lion was alive,
When my courage overflowed,
Why did I not die then!
When I possessed my full strength,
While my mountainlike one was safe,
Why did I not die then?
With pinewood spear and Zulfiqar,
When I shook the world
And held dominion over it,
Why did I not die then?!
When I brought turmoil
Upon all who challenged us,
